Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 55

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Transportation (Bicycle): Bicycle, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Vignette:
Kahu was twelve when the shouting in his house stopped being background noise and became something that could crack the walls. He had come to remember it not as a single night, but as disconnected fragments that never quite fitted together. He felt only parts of the story, an Incomplete Picture that left him wondering what exactly had been broken and whether it would happen again. What frightened him most was the Terror on Recall that rose in his chest the moment he thought of it, exactly as it had felt when he was small and pressed behind the staircase railing. He watched his father’s shadow stretch across the living room carpet, the man’s posture shifting in ways that suggested violence might arrive at any second. When the warm, sweet smell of alcohol drifted down from the kitchen, Kahu’s breath would catch. He was certain that the scent meant the quiet was ending, and he would stay very still until the heavy boots moved away. Over the years, those early fragments solidified into daily habits. Kahu learned to watch other people closely, scanning faces and hands for the subtle signs that others might harm him, a pattern of Watching Others that never fully faded. When he rode his bicycle to client sites, the Transportation felt vulnerable; the physical rhythm of the wheels and the sudden thump of a vehicle backfiring made him Startle to Sounds that ordinary teenagers ignored. At work, where he served as a Project Manager for a regional logistics firm, the open-plan workspace became a place of quiet vigilance. He Avoided People in the breakroom, preferring to step outside or eat at his desk, though the office required him to navigate a steady stream of male colleagues in uniforms and blazers. He had come to believe that staying near the glass partitions and keeping his distance was the safest way to move through the day, especially when he was alone with men in enclosed spaces like the project control room or the back of a delivery van. Kahu smoked throughout the day, and he drank alcohol in the evenings, often taking medication when his shoulders grew tight. These Maladaptive Strategies settled into his routine over weeks and months, becoming so automatic that they shaped his days without demanding conscious effort. He withdrew from social gatherings, telling himself he was simply busy, though he knew he was avoiding the crowds that might bring unpredictable movement. Through it all, his relationship with Elena provided a steady counterweight. She understood his need for routine, and they spent quiet weekends hiking or reading, but Kahu remained hyperaware of male companions. When he rode his bicycle through the city, the olfactory scent of spilled beer from nearby cafes or the Alcohol smell clinging to a colleague’s jacket would trigger a familiar tension in his jaw, the Male Presence in the room sharpening his vigilance. Recently, the accumulation of small moments reached a turning point. Kahu found himself waking before dawn, his mind already scanning for threats, and he began checking that doors and windows were locked, counting the clicks until the metal felt secure. The Fragmented Pieces of his childhood memories no longer felt like a minor inconvenience; they felt like a gap that could swallow him whole. He was most afraid that he would misread a sign, that the quiet before a storm would fool him, and that the terror he had survived would return unannounced. What he hoped for now was not the erasure of the past, but a clearer, more complete picture of what had actually happened. At eighteen, he finally made an appointment, hoping to find a way to manage the watchfulness without letting it steer his life, to breathe through the smoke and the scent of alcohol, and to ride his bicycle through the city without bracing for a blow.
